prompt: The mini-curriculum design in this module borrows a four-part structure directly from this curriculum's own tier design. Which four parts?
choices: Goal, Guided Practice, Checkpoint, Creative Teaching Method
Introduction, Lecture, Quiz, Certificate
Reading, Video, Discussion, Exam
Overview, Theory, Lab, Grade

prompt: In the worked merge-conflict mini-curriculum, why is Lesson 1's goal explicitly 'label which lines are yours/theirs' rather than 'resolve the conflict'?
choices: Labeling is easier to grade automatically than resolving
It separates the diagnosis skill (reading markers) from the treatment skill (resolving), so a failure in resolution can't be confused with a failure in reading
Resolving conflicts requires a checkpoint project, and checkpoints can't appear in Lesson 1
Git does not allow editing a file until all markers are first annotated

prompt: Which of these is an example of specific, useful learner feedback rather than vague praise?
choices: "This was really helpful, thanks! I feel a lot more confident now."
"Great lesson, 10/10, would recommend."

"I didn't need more practice reading markers by lesson 2's end, but once I saw both sides' fixes in conflict C I didn't know how to decide which one was correct -- I needed a step that let me check what each side's tests actually proved before opening the diff."
"I liked the pacing and the examples were clear."

prompt: After Priya's feedback pinpointed confusion specifically in Lesson 2's conflict C, what was the correct scope of the iteration?
choices: Rewrite all four lessons to add more conflict examples throughout, to be thorough
Add one new step (Step 0: check each side's tests before opening the diff) targeted at conflict C only, leaving conflicts A and B unchanged
Remove conflict C entirely since it caused confusion
Add a fifth lesson covering semantic merge conflicts in general theory before Lesson 2

prompt: What makes a target skill for a teach-others-to-learn mini-curriculum well-chosen, according to this module?
choices: It should cover as much ground as possible so the learner gets maximum value
It should be narrow enough that you can tell, within one sitting, whether it transferred -- e.g. resolving one specific class of merge conflict rather than 'learning Git'
It should avoid any checkpoint so the learner doesn't feel tested
It should be a topic the learner already mostly knows, to guarantee a successful session

prompt: This module's assessment note says the Teach-Others-to-Learn capstone is graded primarily on what?
choices: How polished the written lesson plan looks
The real learner's actual results on the checkpoint, not just their satisfaction or praise
Whether the lessons were delivered on the exact planned schedule
Whether an AI assistant reviewed the lesson plan for clarity

prompt: How does this module explicitly close the loop back to Tier 0 of the entire curriculum?
choices: By having the learner retake Tier 0's original quizzes

By pointing out that Tier 0 assumed git mechanics were already known and built communication skills on top; this module has the learner build the same goal/practice/checkpoint/creative-method structure around that exact mechanic (merge) for someone else, turning the former reader of teaching material into its author
By requiring the mini-curriculum to be published as a new Tier 0 module in the official curriculum repository
By having the real learner also complete Tier 0's Specialization Map exercise before the teaching session begins

prompt: In the worked example, why are the three seeded conflicts in Lesson 2 ordered as whitespace-only, then overlapping-added-lines, then semantic (both sides fixed the same bug differently)?
choices: Alphabetical ordering of conflict types is the Git documentation standard
Each step adds exactly one new kind of difficulty rather than several at once, the same ramping principle used elsewhere in this curriculum (e.g. DS&A pattern progression)
Semantic conflicts must always be taught before textual conflicts in Git pedagogy
The order has no pedagogical reasoning behind it; any order would work equally well
